source_refs.note: Book p. 199-200: 6.5 Hyperbola, definition, Figure 6.21, Derivation of the Standard Equation of Hyperbola with Figure 6.22 (up to the start of 6.5.1)

blocks.text: The definition of a hyperbola is similar to that of an ellipse. For an ellipse, the sum of the distances between the foci and a point on the ellipse is fixed, whereas for a hyperbola, the absolute value of the difference between these distances is fixed. One distinguishing feature of a hyperbola is that its graph has two separate branches (see Figure 21).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints "see Figure 21". The figure meant is Figure 6.21 (shown below).

blocks.alt: On a pale yellow panel, the two magenta branches of a hyperbola with foci F' (inside the left branch) and F (inside the right branch); a point P(x, y) on the left branch is joined to F' and F by cyan segments.
blocks.caption: Figure 6.21: The two branches of a hyperbola, a point P(x, y) and the foci F', F (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 6.21)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Ellipse and hyperbola are built from the same ingredients: two fixed points (the foci) and a moving point \(P\). The only change is one word: for the ellipse the SUM \(|PF'| + |PF|\) is constant, for the hyperbola the DIFFERENCE is constant. This one change explains everything that follows: why the curve breaks into two branches, why \(c > a\), why \(e > 1\) and why there are asymptotes. The table below collects these differences; keep it in mind while reading the section.

blocks.caption: Our comparison: ellipse and hyperbola
rows: Sum of the distances from the foci is fixed: \(|PF'| + |PF| = 2a\)
Difference of the distances from the foci is fixed: \(\big||PF'| - |PF|\big| = 2a\)

blocks.text: Derivation of the Standard Equation of Hyperbola

Thus, we can define hyper bola as a hyperbola is the set of all points \((x, y)\) for which the absolute value of the difference between the distances from two distinct fixed points called foci is constant. The hyperbolas with simplest equations are those with foci on one of the coordinate axes. To obtain the simplest equation for a hyperbola, we place the foci on the \(x\)-axis at the points \(F'(-c, 0)\) and \(F(c, 0)\), so that the origin is the midpoint of the segment joining them (see Figure 22).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: "hyper bola" is one word: hyperbola. The sentence should read: "Thus, we can define a hyperbola as the set of all points \((x, y)\) ...". "Figure 22" means Figure 6.22 (below).

blocks.alt: On a pale yellow panel, a cyan hyperbola with centre O on magenta X- and Y-axes; foci F'(-c, 0) and F(c, 0) on the x-axis and a point P(x, y) on the right branch joined to both foci by black segments.
blocks.caption: Figure 6.22: Foci F'(-c, 0), F(c, 0) and a point P(x, y) of the hyperbola (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 6.22)

blocks.text:
Let the absolute value of constant difference of distances from any point \(P(x, y)\) on the hyperbola to the foci be \(2a\), where \(a > 0\). Thus,
\[\big||PF'| - |PF|\big| = 2a\]
or
\[|PF'| - |PF| = \pm 2a\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why call the constant \(2a\) and not just \(a\)? Because then the vertices come out at \(x = \pm a\), exactly like the ellipse; the formulas stay short.
Why \(\pm\)? For a point on the right branch, \(P\) is nearer to \(F\), so \(|PF'| - |PF| = +2a\). For a point on the left branch it is nearer to \(F'\), so the difference is \(-2a\). The \(\pm\) covers both branches at once.

Using the distance formula,
\[\sqrt{(x+c)^2 + y^2} - \sqrt{(x-c)^2 + y^2}\]
\[= \pm 2a\]

To simplify, isolate one radical and square both sides:
\[\sqrt{(x+c)^2 + y^2}\]
\[= \pm 2a + \sqrt{(x-c)^2 + y^2}\]

Expanding the squares,
\[x^2 + 2cx + c^2 + y^2\]
\[= 4a^2 \pm 4a\sqrt{(x-c)^2 + y^2}\]
\[\quad + x^2 - 2cx + c^2 + y^2\]

Cancelling the common terms \(x^2\), \(c^2\), and \(y^2\) from both sides,
\[2cx = 4a^2 \pm 4a\sqrt{(x-c)^2 + y^2}\]
\[\quad - 2cx\]

Bring the terms involving \(cx\) together:
\[4cx = 4a^2 \pm 4a\sqrt{(x-c)^2 + y^2}\]

Divide by 4 and isolate the remaining radical:
\[\mp a\sqrt{(x-c)^2 + y^2} = a^2 - cx\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why isolate a radical before squaring? Squaring \(\sqrt{A} - \sqrt{B}\) directly gives a messy cross term \(-2\sqrt{AB}\), still with roots. With one root alone on a side, squaring removes it completely; the second root is then isolated and removed by a second squaring.
Why \(\mp\)? From \(4cx = 4a^2 \pm 4a\sqrt{\cdots}\), divide by 4: \(cx - a^2 = \pm a\sqrt{\cdots}\). Taking the root term to the left changes its sign, so \(\pm\) becomes \(\mp\). After the next squaring the sign no longer matters.

Now we square both sides again:
\[a^2[(x-c)^2 + y^2]\]
\[= a^4 - 2a^2cx + c^2x^2\]

Adding \(2a^2cx\) to both sides:
\[a^2x^2 + a^2c^2 + a^2y^2 = a^4 + c^2x^2\]

From triangle \(PF'F\) in Figure 2, we note that \(|PF'| - |PF| < |F'F|\), that is, \(2a < 2c\), so \(a < c\) and thus \(a^2 - c^2 < 0\). For convenience, we define a new constant \(b\) such that \(-b^2 = a^2 - c^2\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: "Figure 2" means Figure 6.22 (the triangle \(PF'F\) is drawn there).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The inequality is the triangle inequality: in any triangle, one side is longer than the difference of the other two. In triangle \(PF'F\) the third side is \(|F'F| = 2c\), so \(\big||PF'| - |PF|\big| < 2c\), that is \(2a < 2c\). This is why, for a hyperbola, \(c\) is always bigger than \(a\) (for the ellipse it was the other way round).
Substituting, the equation of the hyperbola becomes \((-b^2)x^2 + a^2y^2 = a^2(-b^2)\).
Finally, dividing both sides by \(-a^2b^2\) gives the standard form of the equation of a hyperbola:

blocks.text_alt: x squared over a squared minus y squared over b squared equals 1

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why introduce \(b\)? Because \(a^2 - c^2\) is negative, and writing it as \(-b^2\) (with \(b > 0\)) gives the neat form above. Dividing by \(-a^2b^2\) turns \(-b^2x^2\) into \(\frac{x^2}{a^2}\) and \(a^2y^2\) into \(-\frac{y^2}{b^2}\).
Memory link: ellipse \(\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\) with \(c^2 = a^2 - b^2\); hyperbola \(\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\) with \(c^2 = a^2 + b^2\). The minus sign in the equation goes with the plus sign in the relation.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A quick numerical check (our example). Take \(a = 3\), \(c = 5\). Then \(b^2 = 25 - 9 = 16\) and the hyperbola is \(\frac{x^2}{9} - \frac{y^2}{16} = 1\). The point \(P\left(5, \frac{16}{3}\right)\) lies on it, because \(\frac{25}{9} - \frac{256}{144} = \frac{25}{9} - \frac{16}{9} = 1\). Its distances from the foci:
\[|PF| = \dfrac{16}{3}\]
\[|PF'| = \sqrt{100 + \dfrac{256}{9}} = \dfrac{34}{3}\]
The difference is \(\frac{34}{3} - \frac{16}{3} = 6 = 2a\), exactly as the definition says.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Hyperbola: \(\big||PF'| - |PF|\big| = 2a\) (difference of distances from the foci is constant).
2. With foci \((\pm c, 0)\): \(\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\), where \(c^2 = a^2 + b^2\).
3. Triangle inequality gives \(a < c\).
4. The graph has two separate branches.
5. Derivation method: isolate a radical, square, simplify, isolate the second radical, square again.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing \(c^2 = a^2 - b^2\) for a hyperbola (that is the ellipse relation). For the hyperbola \(c^2 = a^2 + b^2\).
2. Saying the SUM of distances is constant. For the hyperbola it is the (absolute) DIFFERENCE.
3. Squaring \(\sqrt{A} - \sqrt{B} = 2a\) directly without isolating a root first; the roots do not disappear.
4. Forgetting that \(|PF'| - |PF|\) can be \(+2a\) or \(-2a\) (one sign for each branch).
